title: Rehat and humility
hook: keeping the code does not make one better than others

segments.voice: Yesterday, your rehat: a way of living, chosen on purpose, small enough to start. Your line was my three rules. Which one held, and which one needed a new word? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

Any rule kept well comes with a small, quiet danger. Someone starts running at dawn and, a month later, catches themselves glancing at the people still asleep. Someone gives up sugar and starts noticing everyone else's dessert. Keeping a discipline can turn, without anyone meaning it to, into keeping score. A code as full as the Rehat Maryada, with its articles of faith, its daily banis and its things never to do, could make that danger bigger. A Sikh who keeps every line might be tempted to look sideways at a cousin who doesn't. The hymns speak to that danger. Today is about what they set against it.
screen: `A DISCIPLINE KEPT WELL.` → `A GLANCE AT THE ONES ASLEEP.` → `KEEPING A RULE, OR KEEPING SCORE?`

segments.voice: Begin with Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani Sahib on Ang 266. In paraphrase: the one who knows themselves to be lowly is counted the highest of all. The ladder is turned upside down. Climbing it by your own effort, and announcing it, sends you down. Then Kabir, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own. On Ang 1364, in paraphrase, Kabir says: I am the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands this, he adds, is a friend of mine. That's a startling thing to keep in a holy book. A saint whose words are sung in gurdwaras calls himself the worst. Now a story Sikh tradition tells about the founding of the Khalsa. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. Then, the story goes, he knelt before those same five and asked them to give amrit to him. The Guru received initiation from his own disciples. A line traditionally sung about that day calls him the Guru and the disciple at once. So the founder of the Khalsa put himself under its vow, and under the very people he'd just initiated. Set all three beside the rehat. Read beside these, the code looks like a way to shape a life toward God, not a ranking of who's closer. A Sikh can keep every line and still sit in the langar in the same row as everyone else, eating the same food from the same hands. The rule shapes the one who keeps it. It doesn't make them a judge of anyone who doesn't.
screen: `ANG 266: THE LOWLY COUNTED HIGHEST.` · `ANG 1364: KABIR, THE WORST OF ALL.` · `THE GURU KNEELS TO THE FIVE.` · then, large: `THE RULE SHAPES ME, NOT MY VIEW OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay humble about your practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you do well and keep up: a habit, a skill, a discipline, a prayer. Let yourself feel glad about it for a moment. Then bring to mind someone who doesn't do that thing. Notice whether a little score-keeping shows up. If it does, just see it, without scolding. Then hold that person with the same warmth you just gave your own practice. Let the two sit side by side. The bell holds the time.

Rehat and humility. Keeping the Sikh code doesn't make anyone better than others. The Sukhmani calls the lowly the highest, Kabir calls himself the worst, and tradition says the Guru knelt to his own five. Today's word.

Your line: no better than others. Today, when you catch yourself comparing your effort with someone else's, say one good thing about them instead, out loud or in your head. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching sets humility (nimrata) beside the rehat; in the langar, amritdhari and non-amritdhari Sikhs and visitors sit in the same rows and eat the same food.

fork.setup: you're Guru Gobind Singh. you've just given amrit to five Sikhs and founded the Khalsa. what do you do next?
options: stand above them as the one who initiated them.
kneel and ask the five to give amrit to you.
send them out and keep the vow for them alone.
fork.reveal: tradition says the Guru knelt before the five and received amrit from them, Guru and disciple at once.

original.note: Punjabi: humility. Sikh teaching sets it beside every discipline.

trapdoor: what you thought: people who keep strict religious rules think they're better.
what it means: in Sikh teaching, keeping the code is meant to shape the keeper, not rank them above anyone.
what a scholar hears: the founding story has the Guru receive amrit from the five he initiated, so the Khalsa's founder placed himself under its vow.
recall: the penance for breaking the code

sources.ref: The founding of the Khalsa: the Guru receives amrit from the Panj Pyare

notes: Ang 266, 'aapas kau jo jaanai neecha, sou ganeeai sabh te ooncha', paraphrased; please confirm Ang.
Ang 1364, Kabir's salok 'sabh te ham bure, ham taj bhalo sabh koi; jin aisa kar boojhiaa meet hamaara soi', paraphrased; please confirm Ang and the paraphrase.

The Guru receiving amrit from the Panj Pyare is told as tradition. 'A line traditionally sung about that day calls him the Guru and the disciple at once' refers to the line 'waho waho Gobind Singh, aape gur chela' attributed to Bhai Gurdas (the second); please confirm the attribution and whether to name it.
The phrase 'the first five' for the Panj Pyare: please confirm this is acceptable under the claims rule (the number five is part of the name).
Day 1272 (Who gives amrit) may also have mentioned the founding; this day uses the story only for the Guru kneeling to the five.

Editor pass (1292-1301): counts of articles and kurehats removed (the Rehat Maryada is not cited on this day); 'the first five' and 'the Gurus saw that coming' softened; 'the founder of the code' corrected to 'the founder of the Khalsa' (the written Rehat Maryada is later); the narrator's claim about what the code was 'never meant' to be reframed as a reading of the three texts.
